teaching.causalExplanation: Before Maxwell, electricity and magnetism were already linked. A current makes a magnetic field, and a changing magnetic field makes an electric field. Maxwell added the missing piece. Picture a capacitor charging. No charge crosses the gap between the plates, but the electric field in the gap is growing. Maxwell's equations say that changing electric field makes a magnetic field that curls round the gap, just as a current would. So each kind of field can create the other. One theory now described both. That's what unification means: one set of rules explaining things once treated separately. Now put the two pieces together. A changing electric field makes a changing magnetic field. That changing magnetic field makes a changing electric field, a little further out. And that makes another changing magnetic field, and so on. Each field keeps creating the other, so the disturbance travels by itself. Nothing has to carry it, no air, no water, no medium at all. That's an electromagnetic wave. The electric field and the magnetic field are at right angles to each other, and both are at right angles to the direction the wave travels. So it's a transverse wave. And the two fields rise and fall together, in phase. So what starts the wave? Accelerating charge. In a radio antenna, an alternating voltage drives electrons up and down, many millions of times a second. They speed up, slow down and reverse, so they're always accelerating. Their changing electric field launches the chain of changing fields, and the wave travels outwards. The wave's frequency is the frequency of the charges' oscillation. A charge sitting still has a steady electric field, with no wave. A charge moving at constant velocity is a steady current, with a steady magnetic field, and still no wave. Only accelerating charges radiate.

scenes.teachingReason: Before Maxwell, electricity and magnetism were already linked. A current makes a magnetic field, and a changing magnetic field makes an electric field. scenes.teachingReason: Now put the two pieces together. A changing electric field makes a changing magnetic field. That changing magnetic field makes a changing electric field, a little further out. And that makes another changing magnetic field, and so on. Each field keeps creating the other, so the disturbance travels by itself. Nothing has to carry it, no air, no water, no medium at all. That's an electromagnetic wave. The electric field and the magnetic field are at right angles to each other, and both are at right angles to the direction the wave travels. So it's a transverse wave. And the two fields rise and fall together, in phase.

scenes.teachingReason: So what starts the wave? Accelerating charge. In a radio antenna, an alternating voltage drives electrons up and down, many millions of times a second. They speed up, slow down and reverse, so they're always accelerating. Their changing electric field launches the chain of changing fields, and the wave travels outwards. The wave's frequency is the frequency of the charges' oscillation. A charge sitting still has a steady electric field, with no wave. A charge moving at constant velocity is a steady current, with a steady magnetic field, and still no wave. Only accelerating charges radiate.

scenes.teachingReason: Here's the part that convinced people. Maxwell's equations fix the wave's speed in a vacuum. It's one over the square root of two constants multiplied together. Mu nought, the permeability of free space, sets how strongly currents make magnetic fields. Epsilon nought, the permittivity of free space, sets how strongly charges make electric fields. Both had been measured with coils and capacitors, in experiments that had nothing to do with light. Multiply them, take the square root, and take one over that. You get about three point zero zero times ten to the eight metres per second. That already matched measurements of the speed of light. So Maxwell concluded that light is an electromagnetic wave.
